The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[6–13] "We shall make you recite, so you will not forget, except what God wills. Indeed, He knows what is spoken aloud and what is hidden" (87:6–7). "And We shall ease you toward ease" (87:8). "Then he will neither die therein nor live" (87:13).

"We shall make you recite, so you will not forget" means: We shall make you a reciter, by inspiring you to recite, so that you will not forget what you recite. The meaning is: We shall make you a reciter of the Qur'an, so you will not forget it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: God gave him good news of a clear sign, which is that Jibril would recite to him the revelation he was to recite, while he was illiterate, neither writing nor reading; yet he would memorize it and not forget it.

Notes (tanbihat):

The first: al-Razi said: This verse indicates the miraculous nature (i'jaz) in two respects:

The first: he was an unlettered man, so his memorizing of this lengthy Book without study, repetition, or scribes is beyond the normal course of things, and therefore miraculous.

The second: this surah is among the earliest revealed in Makkah. This is information about a strange and wondrous matter contrary to custom that would occur in the future, and it did occur; thus this is information about the unseen, and therefore miraculous.

The second: It has been said: "(Do not forget)" is a prohibition, and the alif is for pausal lengthening at the end of the verse, which is permissible, like "al-sabilā". The meaning: do not neglect its recitation and repetition, lest you forget it. Thus the prohibition against forgetting is a metaphor for abandoning its voluntary causes.

Al-Razi said: The well-known view is that this is a statement of fact, and the meaning: We shall make you recite until you reach a state where you will not forget and will be secure from forgetting, like your saying: "I will clothe you, so you will not be naked," meaning: so you will be secure from nakedness. Among them: forgetting is not within anyone's power except God's, so commands and prohibitions regarding it are not valid; therefore it must be understood as constancy in those things which exclude forgetting, such as study and frequent recollection, and all of that is a departure from the apparent wording.

Among them: that we take the alif as added for the verse-ending, which is also contrary to the original form.

Among them: if we take it as a statement, the meaning of the verse is God's good news to him that "I will make you such that you will not forget it." If we take it as a prohibition, its meaning is that God commanded him to persist in the means preventing forgetting, namely study and recitation. This does not carry the same good news and exaltation of his status as the first. Moreover, it contradicts His saying: "Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it" (75:16). End.

The third: Al-Burhan al-Shafi'i said in his book (Tafdil al-Salaf 'ala al-Khalaf): Some have mentioned that this verse abrogates the verse: "And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you" (20:114). Its implication confirms the meaning of the other address, because its interpretation is: We shall preserve it for you with a preservation through which you will not fear forgetting; so you have no need to hasten with the Qur'an or move your tongue with it. But they called it abrogation linguistically, not technically, in the sense of a change of state regarding it, for security from forgetting appeared to him after his fear that he would forget it because of moving his tongue with it. End.

His saying, "except what God wills" (87:7), is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of objects: meaning, you will not forget any of the things you recite, except what God wills you to forget, of what human nature sometimes requires.

Al-Zajjaj said: "except what God wills" that he forget: he forgets, then remembers after that, and does not forget completely and permanently; because what is by natural disposition does not change, otherwise the human being would be another world.

It has been said: the exception is figurative, in the sense of paucity intended to convey negation. This is because what is excluded in an exception is less than what remains; and because "what God wills" in common usage is used for the unknown, as if it were said: "except a rare matter that is not known." This is a causal justification for "We shall make you recite," explaining its wisdom: namely, God's prior knowledge of mankind's need for the revelation to be recited to them and for them to be brought through it from darkness to light.

Then He indicated that this recited, revealed matter for action contains no hardship or difficulty, by His saying: "And We shall ease you toward ease" (87:8): meaning, We shall guide you to the easy way, that is, the tolerant, facile Law, which is the easiest of laws and the most suited to the needs of mankind throughout the ages.

"So remind" (87:9): meaning, remind God's servants of His greatness, admonish them, and warn them of His punishment. "If the reminder benefits" (87:9): meaning, the admonition. The "in" (in) here is either in the sense of "since" (idh), as in His saying: "You will have the upper hand if you are believers" (3:139), or in the sense of "qad" ("indeed"), as Ibn Khalawayh said, and supported by His saying: "And remind, for the reminder benefits the believers" (51:55). "He who fears will be reminded" (87:10): meaning, he accepts the reminder and benefits from it. "He who fears" (87:10): meaning, he fears punishment for denial and obstinacy after the proof has become evident.

"But the most wretched will avoid it" (87:11), "He who will burn in the greatest Fire" (87:12): meaning, the greatest in pain and torment.

"Then he will neither die therein nor live" (87:13): meaning, he will not perish so as to find rest, nor will he live a life that benefits him. It has been said: when the Arabs described a man as having fallen into a severe hardship, they would say: "He is neither alive nor dead," so this came in line with their customary speech.
